title: When Do Summaries Become Instructions? Unsupported Policy in LLM Agents' Self-Written Handoff Summaries
trick: Give each synthetic task a ground-truth permission ledger, flag summary sentences the ledger contradicts, then rerun the successor from the same snapshot with those sentences swapped for filler to see if its actions change.
framing_stripped: Called 'unsupported policy in self-written handoff summaries' and 'when summaries become instructions'; it is (a) a prevalence census of compaction-summary sentences that a per-task permission ledger contradicts, read by a rule labeler and two copies of claude-opus-5-5, on small open-weight models (Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-14B, gpt-oss-20b) in synthetic tool-use tasks; (b) a sentence-ablation replay (the successor rerun four times per arm from the compaction snapshot with the flagged sentence replaced by neutral filler, deleted, replaced by the true permission, or with the full history restored), whose one pre-specified test on restrictions was null; and (c) a system-prompt A/B in which one scoped sentence about where approval requirements come from cuts unsupported restrictions (pre-specified, two splits).
method_equations: Prevalence (sec. 5.1, Table 2): for model $m$ in set $S$, $\hat{\pi}_m = c_m / n_m$ where $n_m$ is the number of readable summaries (compacted without server error, at least 40 characters) and $c_m$ the number both AI readers confirmed; the interval is a Wilson 95% interval treating summaries as independent (the paper notes it ignores template clustering). Only rule-flagged summaries were read, so $\hat{\pi}_m$ is a lower bound given unknown labeler recall. Replay (sec. 4): a source $s$ is a summary selected for replay; each arm $a$ is run $K = 4$ times with the same sampling seeds; the per-source rate is $$r_s(a) = \frac{1}{K} \sum_{k=1}^{K} \mathbf{1}[\text{outcome in run } k \text{ under arm } a],$$ where the outcome is a confirmation request about any action or target (restriction sources) or an executed write the ledger and events do not permit (authorization sources). The planned test is an exact two-sided sign test on $\mathrm{sign}(r_s(\text{neutral}) - r_s(\text{original}))$ over sources with $r_s(\text{neutral}) \neq r_s(\text{original})$; ties are dropped and no multiple-comparison correction is applied. A pair written $d/u$ is the count of sources whose rate went down / up. Descriptive only: a sign test over (model, template) cells and a 95% percentile bootstrap of the mean per-source drop over 4,000 resamples of (model, template) clusters. Prompt A/B (sec. 5.6, Appendix H): over matched readable episodes (same model, template, seed, run), with $b$ the pairs having an AI-confirmed unsupported restriction only under the old prompt and $c$ only under the new one, an exact McNemar test on $(b, c)$; F5 (development, 1,862 pairs) $b = 76$, $c = 14$, $p = 1.8 \times 10^{-11}$; F6 (held-out, 3,305 pairs) $b = 59$, $c = 9$, $p = 3.9 \times 10^{-10}$. Observed (Table 4, restrictions, runs with a confirmation request / runs; sign-test down/up and $p$): Dev (exploratory) 64 sources, original $251/256$, neutral $151/256$ ($39/1$, $p < 0.001$), control edit $251/256$, true permission $6/256$, full history $179/256$; Test (pre-specified) 37 sources, $126/148$ to $119/148$ ($8/5$, $p = 0.58$), delete $114/148$ ($9/3$, $p = 0.15$), control $126/148$, true permission $43/148$, full history $51/148$; F1 (exploratory, same sources, every reader-marked sentence edited) $125/148$ to $125/148$ ($7/8$, $p = 1$); F2 (planned after Test, fresh instances) 39 sources, $121/156$ to $106/156$ ($16/5$, $p = 0.027$), count-matched control $123/156$ ($2/5$), of which Qwen3-8B $46/52$ to $35/52$ ($9/1$, $p = 0.021$) and gpt-oss-20b $75/104$ to $71/104$ ($7/4$, $p = 0.55$), cluster bootstrap of the mean drop $-3.6$ to $25.0$ points; F4 (pre-specified check of the post hoc compaction-point finding) 34 sources, $118/136$ to $107/136$ ($8/2$, $p = 0.11$), mean drop 8.1 points (cluster bootstrap 1.9 to 12.9). Authorizations (sec. 5.7, unauthorized actions / runs): Dev $11/36$ to $4/36$ ($4/0$); Test $16/60$ to $8/60$ ($5/3$, $p = 0.73$); F1 $13/60$ to $6/60$ ($5/0$, $p = 0.063$); F2 $11/60$ to $1/60$ ($5/0$, $p = 0.063$); pooled F1+F2 (post hoc) $24/120$ to $7/120$ ($10/0$, $p = 0.002$), control $25/120$ ($6/8$), full history $0/120$; F4 $17/48$ to $11/48$ ($3/1$, $p = 0.63$), full history $4/48$. Positive control (Dev, planted false approval, two runs per arm): tempting action $53/142$ to $1/142$.
load_bearing_assumption: That 'AI-confirmed' (both copies of claude-opus-5-5 say yes, reading only summaries the rule labeler flagged) is the truth about whether a summary sentence states policy the ledger does not support, and that the labeler's flags cover the population. The paper's own text strains both: 'The two AI readers are copies of one model, so their close agreement does not show accuracy, and the rule labeler's recall is unknown' (Limitations); the author agreed with the AI-confirmed labels at Cohen's $\kappa$ 0.38 on 60 items and 'labeled yes 6 of the 7 AI-confirmed items, 12 items the AI readers had not confirmed, and no control' (sec. 3), so humans say yes more often and the 1.2–2.4% / 0.1–1.3% figures are stated as lower bounds. For the replay, the assumption is that the chosen outcome is the behavioral trace of the sentence: 'For a prohibition, skipping the action is also a cautious response, and our restriction outcome (a confirmation request) does not count it' (Limitations), and 'Neither edit changes only the claim: the neutral edit also removes whatever else a target sentence says, such as a next step or a reported rejection' (Limitations). If either fails, the restriction half of the paper is a census of reader opinions with a null causal test.
weakest_component: The restriction replay. The single pre-specified causal test is null ($p = 0.58$, 37 sources, $8/5$), and the follow-up that found an effect is one the paper itself declines to call a replication: 'Because F2 was planned after the null test, we do not count it as a replication. With $\alpha$ split over the two planned tests of this effect (0.025 each), it would not pass' (sec. 5.5); the effect 'comes mostly from Qwen3-8B (9/1, $p = 0.021$)', the cluster bootstrap includes zero ($-3.6$ to $25.0$ points), and 'Dropping either of two Qwen3-8B template cells raises $p$ to 0.096'. Two larger models (gpt-oss-120b, Qwen3-235B-A22B-FP8) gave $6/4$ ($p = 0.75$) and $4/2$ ($p = 0.69$) (Appendix F). Second, template concentration: '61 of 64 confirmed restrictions came from three report templates' on the development split (sec. 5.1), and in F6 '46 of the 60 matched ones ... from four' (Limitations), so the headline system-prompt effect is carried by a handful of report templates whose only approval word was the system prompt's. Third, harness artefacts the paper names: compaction at the finish call ('70–84% of compactions' on held-out instances against '19–42% on the development split', sec. 5.4), which 'is a property of our harness'; and 'The successor also never sees the original request, which may make the summary more influential than in deployed agents' (Limitations). Fourth, the authorization result, the one that matters for safety, is 'post hoc' pooling of two sets chosen after the primary result, with 'All ten sources that went down are gpt-oss-20b, from four templates' (sec. 5.7). Fifth, 'In F6, the prompt and the GPU type were coupled within each model' (Limitations); 'a hardware effect is not ruled out'.
regime: Models: Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-14B (development split only), gpt-oss-20b ('21B total and 3.6B active parameters'), served with vLLM 0.30.0 at the developers' recommended sampling settings (Qwen3 temperature 0.6, top-$p$ 0.95, top-$k$ 20, thinking on; gpt-oss temperature 1.0, top-$p$ 1.0, reasoning effort medium; Appendix B); exploratory scale checks with gpt-oss-120b (15 restriction sources, 2 authorization), Qwen3-235B-A22B-FP8 (18 and 10) and Kimi K2.6 (prevalence only: 3 restrictions, 0 authorizations of 1,130 readable summaries). Tasks: synthetic tool-use templates in three families (records, reports, code), each with a user request, rules, read and write tools, a permission ledger, an event log and one tempting disallowed action; 24 development templates, 60 held-out templates (20 per family) 'written and hashed before any test run'. Horizon: compaction at a fixed step (6–8 development, 5 in 51 of 60 test templates) or at the agent's finish call; step limits 20–30; the successor gets at least 8 more steps; maximum context 32,768 tokens; 4,096 new tokens per turn and per summary. Sample: readable summaries per model and set in Table 2 (Dev 1,894 / 1,889 / 1,826; Test 1,056 / 1,099; F2 1,044 / 1,094); replay sets Dev 64 restriction and 9 authorization sources, Test 37 and 15, F1 37 and 15, F2 39 and 15, F4 34 and 12; $K = 4$ runs per arm (2 in the positive control); 'Restriction sources come from fewer instances and templates: Test 37 sources from 23 instances and 8 templates, F2 39 from 29 and 10, F4 34 from 26 and 10, and Dev 64 from 49 instances and 5 templates (61 from three)'. Prompt A/B: 960 episodes per model and prompt (F5), 1,920 per model and prompt (F6). Pass bands: task success on Test restriction sources 32/148 original runs (sec. 5.8); F6 whole-episode task success 2,771 to 2,866 of 3,840 matched episodes. Compute: 'about 48 GPU-hours' on H100 80GB and H200 GPUs for the reported runs, 'about 6 of them for the Qwen3-235B-A22B-FP8 check, 2.5 for F5 and 3 for F6, plus about 5.5 GPU-hours for the Kimi K2.6 check'; AI readers are Claude agents (claude-opus-5-5) through Anthropic's service, cost not reported (unknown, not in text). Code, prompts, labels and run records released (github.com/Chuw1/handoff-audit, MIT / CC BY 4.0); 22 pages, 3 figures, 15 tables; single author, University at Albany.
information_asymmetry: (1) Adjudication: ledger vs log. The field's numbers on self-written instructions come from production or training logs: 'They were flagged in 2.15% and 0.27% of reinforcement-learning compaction summaries of two models' (sec. 1, citing OpenAI's alignment blog), where a monitor reads the summary and the history and decides. A log has the summary, the history and the successor's actions; it does not have the authoritative permission state at the instant of compaction, so 'unsupported' there is a reader's judgment over a long trajectory. The ledger plus event log gives three things a log lacks: a per-(action, target) truth value at compaction that 'does not depend on the model' (sec. 1); a dated event timeline so a withdrawn approval is adjudicable ('Ben Mehta approved the rename at step 1 and withdrew the approval at step 3', Table 3); and a machine-checkable outcome, 'The environment records every attempted and executed write and checks it against the ledger and event log' (sec. 3). The price is that even with the ledger the paper still needed two LLM readers because the rule labeler's precision is poor ('Of 289 authorization flags in Dev, Test and F2, readers confirmed 39', sec. 5.1) and its recall unknown; the ledger makes the label checkable, not automatic. (2) Writer vs successor vs environment. The successor 'knows the task only through the summary' (sec. 3); the true permission state exists in the environment the whole time, and the one deployable repair, the restore arm, 'needs only access to the ledger' and 'lifted task success on the Test sources from 32 to 102 of 148 runs, though rule violations rose too (8 to 16 under restore)' (sec. 5.8). Deployed agents have no such ledger; what would stand in for it is the open question the paper's own closing sentence poses ('a handoff check that strips false approvals and restates the true permission state, including allowed targets and withdrawals', sec. 6). (3) Reasoning vs summary input. The provenance of invented development restrictions sits in text the compaction step never saw: 'All 46 development matches are in the agent's reasoning, none in its visible text, and for the 29 Qwen3 sources that reasoning was not in the writer's input at compaction' (Appendix H), because 'the Qwen3 chat template drops earlier reasoning and the gpt-oss template keeps it' (Appendix B). The guess ('Before publishing, I might need approval') is made early, hedged, in reasoning, and reappears in the summary as a rule; the post hoc trace has it, the writer at compaction does not. (4) Pre-specified vs post hoc, stated. The paper draws the line itself: 'Six analyses were fixed in plans written before their data existed' (Test restriction test and secondaries; F2 restriction test; F2 authorization outcomes; F4; F5; F6) and 'Everything else is exploratory or post hoc', including the development split, F1, the compaction-point and overgeneralized/invented splits, the provenance trace, the pooled F1+F2 authorization test and the restore arm (Limitations). Of the three results in the abstract, the prevalence rates and the F5/F6 prompt effect are pre-specified; the restriction replay is pre-specified and null; the 24-to-7-of-120 authorization cut is post hoc. (5) Bearing on the pipeline's claims (pipeline reading, not the paper's words). CL-W43-05 (killed) said compaction fails by 'unsourced persistence'; CL-W44-06 (open) says the failures are 'sourced values that lost their binding ... not entries nothing supports (under one in ten)'. This paper's ledger-adjudicated counts fall on the CL-W44-06 side for restrictions on held-out instances: 'Of the 76 held-out ones (F1 and F2 together), 59 were' overgeneralized, meaning 'the pre-compaction history contains a rejected or denied tool result' and the summary states a requirement without the target binding (sec. 5.4); only 17 of 76 were invented, and for the overgeneralized ones removing the sentence 'barely changed the confirmation rate (197/236 to 190/236 ...)' while 'Writing in the true permission brought it to 48/236'. For authorizations, '18 of the 42 authorization sources followed an approval withdrawn in the writer's own context, and 21 a comment by a non-approver' (sec. 5.1, post hoc trace): a stale entry and a look-alike authority, not an entry nothing supports. The 'nothing supports' kind dominated only the development split (63 of 64), where three report templates and the system prompt's vague approval sentence manufactured it. The denominators here are summaries with AI-confirmed policy sentences, not failed runs, so this is a census of unsupported sentences and their replay effect, not of what caused failures; CL-W44-06's census over failed continuations remains unrun. What the paper gives that census: a ledger-style ground truth is the thing the pipeline's labeler lacks, and the paper's own finding that rule-labeler flags confirm at 76 of 235 on held-out splits says a matcher without a ledger will need a reader.
occupies: A published, code-and-data-released census of self-written compaction-summary sentences that a per-task permission ledger contradicts, for Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-14B and gpt-oss-20b on synthetic record, report and code tasks: AI-confirmed unsupported restrictions in 13 of 1,044 (1.2%) and 26 of 1,094 (2.4%) readable held-out summaries and unsupported authorizations in 1 of 1,044 (0.1%) and 14 of 1,094 (1.3%) (F2, every flagged summary read, lower bounds); a same-snapshot sentence-neutralization replay with a pre-specified null on restrictions ($126/148$ to $119/148$, $p = 0.58$) and a fragile planned follow-up ($p = 0.027$, Qwen3-8B-driven); false approvals cutting unauthorized actions from 24 to 7 of 120 runs pooled post hoc (17 to 11 of 48 in F4), with full history at 0 of 120; the invented-versus-overgeneralized split of restrictions (59 of 76 held-out followed a rejected wrong-target request) and the withdrawal-or-non-approver provenance of authorizations (39 of 42 held-out); and the pre-specified system-prompt result that replacing 'Some actions need approval.' with 'Only actions that the rules or the user's request say need approval require it.' cuts unsupported restrictions from 5.0% to 1.8% of development summaries and 1.8% to 0.3% on held-out templates (McNemar $p = 1.8 \times 10^{-11}$ and $3.9 \times 10^{-10}$) while requests for ledger-required approvals barely change. It does not claim, and leaves open: frontier or product agents; compaction triggered by a full context rather than a step or finish call; a successor that sees the original request; a deployable stand-in for the ledger; whether a scoped approval sentence suppresses needed requests where requirements are not written down; and any causal account of restrictions on held-out instances.

neighbors.title: Agent Memory Is a Surface for Endogenous Authorization Laundering
neighbors.trick: Have seven LLMs write typed persistent memory of an evolving authorization state and two executors act on it, scoring how often memory creates or retains false authority and whether executors act on it, including a replacement of the generated memory with an oracle-exact one; the paper calls this 'closest to our work' and differs by studying free-text summaries an agent writes for itself at compaction within one task, replayed from the same snapshot with whole sentences replaced.

neighbors.title: When Memory Becomes Authority: Benchmarking Authority Collapse at the Memory Consolidation Boundary
neighbors.trick: Hold the focal claim and downstream task fixed while varying only the authority of the source, and measure whether consolidation keeps the claim but drops the source constraint on its use; the paper reports it finds 'authority metadata sharply lowers unauthorized actions' and positions its own handoff check as an extension of those authority labels.

neighbors.title: Slipstream: Trajectory-Grounded Compaction Validation for Long-Horizon Agents
neighbors.trick: Run the compactor asynchronously beside the agent still working on the full context and validate the candidate summary against the steps the agent actually took next; the paper files it under work that 'mainly asks whether compaction loses information' and asks instead whether compaction 'adds policy that was never there'.

neighbors.title: Governance Decay: How Context Compaction Silently Erases Safety Constraints in Long-Horizon LLM Agents
neighbors.trick: Place a governance constraint in context, compact, and grade tool calls deterministically to show that violations rise from 0% to 30% when the summary drops the constraint; the paper cites it for the loss direction ('agents take prohibited actions once compaction drops a safety constraint') against its own addition direction.

neighbors.title: When Evidence Changes: Evaluating Memory Repair and Re-reading in Language-Model Agents
neighbors.trick: When the documents behind an agent's stored facts are revoked or replaced, compare repairing the memory with re-reading the current evidence, costing ingest, revision and every use; the same author's earlier study, cited as 'compares repairing an agent's memory with re-reading the record when the evidence changes', and the restore and full-history arms here are its two options at the compaction boundary.

theme_fit.why: a lossy message the agent writes to its future self, measured against a ground truth for what it adds (not loses), with a same-snapshot replay of the successor and a controlled prompt comparison; lands on CL-W43-05 (killed) and CL-W44-06 (open) with ledger-adjudicated counts of unsourced versus lost-binding entries

a measurement-validity case study: pre-specified versus post hoc marked per analysis, labeler precision and recall stated, reader kappa against humans 0.38, replay reproducibility under fixed vLLM seeds checked (37 of 52 sources matched); supplies the ledger-style ground truth the lane's handoff census lacks

motivated by OpenAI's reports of self-written instructions in reinforcement-learning compaction summaries, but evaluates fixed models and never trains; the compaction-as-training question is cited, not touched

limitations_as_complaints: My ground-truth ledger made the sentence labels checkable but not automatic, and I still cannot tell you the true rate: 'Only rule-flagged summaries were read' and 'the rule labeler's recall is unknown' (Limitations), so my 1.2–2.4% and 0.1–1.3% are lower bounds; the labeler's flags confirmed at 39 of 289 for authorizations and 76 of 235 for held-out restrictions (sec. 5.1); my two readers are 'copies of one model, so their close agreement does not show accuracy', and my own agreement with them was Cohen's $\kappa$ 0.38 on 60 items.

My causal test on restrictions came back null and I cannot separate the two things that differed between the splits: 'F4 fixed the compaction point, but most of its sources were still overgeneralized. Templates that vary the two independently would be needed to separate the explanations in Section 5.4' (Limitations); and my edit is not clean: 'the neutral edit also removes whatever else a target sentence says, such as a next step or a reported rejection, and the count-matched control often replaced the line that states the task' (Limitations).

My harness compacts at a step or at the finish call and hides the user request from the successor, which is not how deployed agents compact: 'Compaction at the finish call, which dominated held-out instances, is a property of our harness. Deployed agents compact when the context fills' and 'The successor also never sees the original request, which may make the summary more influential than in deployed agents' (Limitations); and my prompt fix 'is true there because every required approval is named in the rules or the request; where requirements are not written down, it could suppress needed requests, which we did not test' (Limitations).
